newsitem.title: CANADA: Unity cloud hangs over Canadian provincial premiers.
newsitem.headline: Unity cloud hangs over Canadian provincial premiers.

text.p: Like swimmers beside a pool, Canada's provincial premiers on Friday dipped their toes into the frosty debate over national unity and considered whether to take the plunge.

The leaders of the nine English-speaking provinces said they expected to discuss the process for resolving the issue of national unity but would avoid any debate that would anger separatist premier Lucien Bouchard of mainly French-speaking Quebec.
The nine premiers hailed Thursday's agreement to "rebalance" the provincial-federal relationship in managing key social programs while downplaying Quebec's refusal to go along with the proposal.

"These things don't happen in a vacuum ... Quebec knew what was in the (proposal) paper. We knew Quebec's views. They knew what we were going to say," host premier Frank McKenna told reporters on Friday.

The proposal, championed by Ontario Premier Mike Harris, would give the provinces more say in managing of key social programs and perhaps place limits on the Canadian federal government's spending power.
Bouchard refused to support the measure because of the control it would still gave Canada's federal government over Quebec's affairs.

"Quebec cannot accept this and I am convinced that no one in Quebec could contradict me were I to say that this is a constant element of our policy and of our perception of what Quebecers are," Bouchard told reporters Thursday.

National unity is not on the meeting's agenda -- at Bouchard's insistence -- but the issue has hung like a cloud over this seaside resort since the provincial leaders arrived on Wednesday. The meeting is scheduled to end today.

Saskatchawan premier Roy Romanow told reporters on Friday he planned to push the issue, echoing Alberta Premier Ralph Klein who also used a television interview on Thursday to blast the federal government's handling of the Quebec issue.
McKenna, however, said he doubted the premiers would get in to a detailed discussion of changing Canada's constitution to meet Quebec's concerns.

"My impression is that the premiers would like to avoid any in depth debate. There will probably be a discussion around issue of process, around the launching of the debate on the issue (of unity,) McKenna said.
Bouchard has threatened to walk out of the meetings if there is a discussion on national unity.
